questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Apply the product and quotient laws of indices to simplify expressions
questions.stepByStepExplanation: When multiplying powers with the same base, add the indices: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. Here m = 3 and n = 4, so a³ × a⁴ = a⁷.
questions.commonMisconception: Students often multiply the indices (3 × 4 = 12) instead of adding them.
questions.aiTutorContext: Student is practising basic index laws. Emphasize same-base rule: multiply → add indices. Use football score analogies if preferred explanation style is football.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.commonMisconception: Adding indices (2 + 5 = 7) instead of multiplying for power of a power.
questions.aiTutorContext: Focus on power-of-a-power: multiply the indices. Contrast with product rule where indices are added.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.stepByStepExplanation: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. Therefore 3⁻² = 1/3² = 1/9. The negative sign applies to the index, not the value.
questions.commonMisconception: Treating 3⁻² as -9 or -1/9 by attaching the minus sign to the result.
questions.aiTutorContext: Clarify that negative index means reciprocal, not a negative number. Compare 3² = 9 vs 3⁻² = 1/9.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Simplify surds by extracting square factors
questions.commonMisconception: Writing √50 = 25√2 by multiplying instead of taking the square root of the perfect-square factor.
questions.aiTutorContext: Teach the pattern: pull out perfect squares. Practice factoring the number under the radical first.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Rationalise a denominator containing a single surd
questions.commonMisconception: Forgetting to simplify 6√3 / 3 after rationalising, or multiplying only the denominator.
questions.aiTutorContext: Show why we multiply by the surd: to create a rational denominator. Always simplify the resulting fraction.
